prompt:
A 71-year-old man with newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 28%, nonischemic after a normal coronary angiogram) and permanent atrial fibrillation is seen 1 week after discharge. His medications are furosemide 40 mg daily, diltiazem ER 240 mg daily (started years ago for rate control), and apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and he takes naproxen for gout flares. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, heart rate 92 and irregular, with mild ankle edema; weight is 82 kg. Creatinine is 1.7 mg/dL (eGFR 41), potassium 5.0 mEq/L, and sodium 136 mEq/L. He feels better than on admission but still gets dyspneic walking one block. How would you optimize his regimen?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Discontinue diltiazem because nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers worsen outcomes in reduced ejection fraction.
Start an evidence-based beta-blocker such as metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, or bisoprolol at a low dose and titrate every 2 weeks.
Stop naproxen and advise avoidance of all NSAIDs.
Start an SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin.
Start low-dose sacubitril/valsartan, or an ACE inhibitor or ARB if an ARNI is not feasible.
Defer mineralocorticoid antagonist initiation until potassium is below 5.0 mEq/L and renal function is stable, then start low-dose spironolactone.
Recheck creatinine and potassium within 1 to 2 weeks after each renin-angiotensin or mineralocorticoid antagonist change.
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily because he meets only one dose-reduction criterion.
Treat gout flares with renally adjusted low-dose colchicine or a short corticosteroid course instead of NSAIDs.
Consider low-dose allopurinol titrated to target uric acid for recurrent flares once the acute flare settles.
Adjust the furosemide dose to volume status guided by daily weights.
Counsel daily weights and to call for a gain of more than 2 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week.
Counsel moderate dietary sodium restriction.
Consider low-dose digoxin as add-on rate control if heart rate remains uncontrolled on a beta-blocker, with renal dosing and level monitoring.
Repeat echocardiography after about 3 months of optimized therapy to reassess ejection fraction before any ICD decision.
Consider tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy and refer to electrophysiology to discuss rhythm control if rate control remains inadequate.
Refer to a heart failure clinic and cardiac rehabilitation.
Update influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccinations.
Check iron studies and treat iron deficiency with intravenous iron when indicated.
Check thyroid function if not already done as part of the cardiomyopathy evaluation.
Obtain ambulatory ECG monitoring to assess 24-hour rate control.
Schedule follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks for medication titration.
Counsel on SGLT2 inhibitor sick-day rules and genital hygiene.
Continue diltiazem and add a beta-blocker.
Increase diltiazem to improve rate control.
Continue naproxen at a lower dose for gout flares.
Start spironolactone 25 mg now despite potassium of 5.0 mEq/L and eGFR 41.
Start sacubitril/valsartan together with an ACE inhibitor.
Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily because of renal function.
Replace apixaban with aspirin.
Start dronedarone for rhythm control.
Start flecainide for rhythm control.
Add a routine potassium supplement with the loop diuretic.
Prescribe a high-dose colchicine loading regimen for gout flares.
Discontinue furosemide entirely because edema is mild and creatinine is elevated.
Withhold all renin-angiotensin inhibition because eGFR is below 45.
Start ivabradine to lower heart rate.
Refer for immediate primary-prevention ICD implantation before optimizing medical therapy.
Advise drinking at least 3 liters of fluid daily to protect the kidneys.
